title: A down jacket makes no heat at all. So why does it keep you warm? | So That's Why
description:
On a cold-snap morning you take your down jacket out of the closet, and it feels cold. It has no plug and no battery, and it makes no heat of its own. So why does it keep you warm once you put it on?

In this episode, the Chief and Little Q follow one down jacket to find the heater: where the heat comes from, why it keeps running away, why the iron railing in a park feels colder than the wooden bench in the same park, what blocks heat best, and why down stops keeping you warm when it's squashed, soaked or blown through by wind. At the end, a vacuum flask and a wrapped-up ice cube show what keeping warm really does.

The illustrations in this episode were made with AI. The power figures and multiples are typical textbook values or rough orders of magnitude; the source of every claim is listed in the references below.

p001.text: Chief! So cold! I open my closet,

p002.text: and my down jacket is cold!

p003.text: Isn't it supposed to be warm? Why's it cold?

p004.text: Easy now. Feel your own hand. It's warm, right?

p005.text: Warm. But it's not plugged in,

p006.text: so why's it warm once I wear it?

p007.text: Where does the heat come from?

p008.text: Hmm, the answer's closer than you think.

p009.text: Guess: wrap ice in a down jacket.

p010.text: Will it melt faster, or slower?

p011.text: Why does the park's iron railing feel so much colder than the wooden bench?

p012.text: And why does a wet down jacket stop being warm so fast?

p013.text: A cold jacket... why's it warm on me?

p014.text: Try this: put a thermometer in a down jacket overnight.

p017.text: So it's as cold as the chair in the room?

p018.text: Yes. Chairs, tables, this jacket: given time, they match the room.

p019.text: Colder than your hand, so they feel cold.

p021.text: Fair guess. It really feels like it makes heat.

p022.text: But open it up: just down and fabric inside.

p023.text: If it made heat, the thermometer would've shown it.

p027.text: Me? I'm not burning a fire.

p028.text: Your body uses what you eat.

p029.text: So eating is like adding firewood?

p031.text: Most of the energy it uses ends up as heat.

p032.text: An adult sitting quietly gives off about 100 watts of heat,

p034.text: So I'm a light bulb too?

p035.text: Kids are smaller and give off less,

p036.text: but you never stop. Even asleep, you just give off a bit less.

p037.text: What about when I'm shivering with cold?

p039.text: Shivering can make several times the heat of sitting still.

p040.text: Next time you shiver, tell yourself:

p042.text: But I make heat all day,

p043.text: so why do I still get cold?

p045.text: it always flows from hot to cold.

p046.text: Hold hot cocoa: heat flows from the cup into your hands.

p047.text: Hold ice: your hand gets cold and the ice melts.

p048.text: So the ice gives me its cold?

p049.text: The other way: your hand's heat goes into the ice.

p050.text: Cold doesn't move. Heat is what moves.

p052.text: Not on its own. Ice never makes your hand warmer.

p053.text: On cold tiles barefoot, heat leaves your feet for the floor.

p056.text: Hold that thought. The park will tell.

p057.text: So cold is just heat always running away?

p058.text: Right. Clothes can't stop it, only slow it.

p062.text: Sounds right. But they spent all night in the same park,

p064.text: No way! They feel so different.

p066.text: Your hand feels how fast heat leaves it.

p067.text: Iron carries heat off your hand fast; wood carries it slowly.

p068.text: Steel's over 100 times faster than wood.

p069.text: Rugs and tiles are the same: tiles carry heat from your feet faster.

p070.text: The zipper's colder than cloth, too!

p071.text: But hold it a moment and it isn't cold: your heat has gone in.

p072.text: Next time something feels cold, ask:

p073.text: is it really colder, or just great at carrying heat away?

p075.text: This may surprise you: the best heat blocker around you is air.

p076.text: Air? We're soaking in air every day!

p078.text: The trouble is, air hates staying still.

p080.text: Air next to you gets warm and floats up,

p081.text: cold air moves in, and heat gets carried off.

p082.text: Why does warm air float up?

p083.text: It's lighter than cold air, so it rises.

p084.text: Even standing still, heat keeps leaving you.

p085.text: So the jacket's warm because feathers are warm?

p086.text: Down actually carries heat about as well as air.

p088.text: it's a tangle of super-fine threads, spreading out every way.

p089.text: Packed together, they prop open tons of tiny spaces.

p090.text: Air gets trapped in them and can't float away.

p091.text: So why not just wear air?

p092.text: Open air swirls around and takes heat off.

p093.text: Cut it into tiny cells, and it can't swirl.

p095.text: A down jacket is a coat full of air!

p097.text: the key material is air, and air is free.

p098.text: Your sweater and your quilt use the same trick: trap air.

p100.text: Yes. Animal fur traps air in it too.

p101.text: What if I squash my jacket?

p102.text: Hug it hard, and the spot you hug goes flat.

p105.text: What if I sit on it?

p106.text: Then the bit under your bottom is flattest.

p107.text: So heavier and thicker always means warmer?

p109.text: It's how much still air is trapped inside.

p110.text: And if it gets rained on?

p113.text: Water carries heat 20-some times better than air.

p114.text: Wet clothes let heat out much faster, so they're less warm.

p115.text: Wet down collapses; the spaces close.

p116.text: Winter rain: you know that cold.

p118.text: Yes. And as water dries, it takes even more heat from you.

p119.text: Why is it so cold when it's windy?

p122.text: cold air swaps in, heat leaves faster.

p123.text: Wind often takes heat far faster than slow contact.

p124.text: That's wind chill: same temperature, much colder with wind.

p125.text: Wind chill is about bare skin: your face, ears, and hands.

p126.text: No wonder my ears hurt first!

p127.text: So the jacket's outer layer should block wind,

p131.text: Wind pours in and blows your warm air away.

p134.text: so how does ice water stay cold?

p135.text: A flask and a down jacket do the same job.

p136.text: It doesn't heat or cool; heat just can't easily get through.

p137.text: A flask is two bottles, with the air between nearly all gone.

p140.text: Right. Jacket air can't move, but heat still creeps by;

p141.text: the flask is nearly empty there; heat barely crosses.

p142.text: So a flask is a super down jacket?

p143.text: Sort of, except you can't wear it.

p144.text: Is the neck like my open zipper?

p145.text: Pretty much. No vacuum at the neck, so much heat slips out there.

p146.text: So it keeps hot soup hot and ice water cold!

p147.text: Yes. Remember heat's rule? Whichever way it runs, the flask blocks it.

p148.text: And a down jacket in summer?

p150.text: In summer you don't want that, so you'd roast.

p152.text: It's so warm, it'll melt faster, right?

p153.text: Many guess that, but there's no heater inside.

p154.text: Remember the thermometer night? It didn't warm up at all.

p155.text: Lots of classrooms try this: one cube wrapped, one not.

p159.text: It's warm because it keeps MY heat in!

p161.text: that little wait is your heat filling it up.

p163.text: Ice cream in a down jacket: melts faster, or slower?
